new_statements.rule_in_words: Okpe is described as a tone language with two level tones (High, Low) plus a downstepped High (whose status -- downstepped H vs raised L -- Omamor leaves open); nouns carry lexical melodies (e.g. verbal nouns L-H / L-H-L), verbs take their tones from the syntactic context. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent; none states where stress falls or that it is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: Omamor 1988 n.6 is uncertain whether the third pitch is a downstepped H or a raised L; Elugbe 1989 p.48 notes SWE languages lack downdrift but have downstep and a final-low-raising phenomenon.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone marking on nouns, verbal nouns and inflected verb forms; verbs unmarked in citation form. Nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Okpe [oke] = Glottolog okpe1250, South-Western Edoid (with Urhobo, Uvwie, Isoko, Eruwa), spoken in Okpe LGA, Delta State; speakers call themselves Urhobo but the language is distinct (Elugbe 1989 p.15, Omamor 1988 p.47). Omamor 1988 does not name a dialect; Elugbe 1989 sec. 4.6 rests on one informant, Solomon Enunuaye. Not the identically named North-Western Edoid Okpe [okx] = okpe1249 (Akoko-Edo; Decker et al. 2024 and Lewis 2013 concern that language).

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent/prominence (0 hits in scanned). Tone only: p.57 verbal nouns from monosyllabic verbs have a LOW-HIGH tonal shape, from disyllabic verbs LOW-HIGH-LOW; Notes p.61: tones marked High, Low and ! downstepped high; n.6 says the downstep follows Hoffmann 1973 and the author is unsure whether it is a downstepped high or a raised low; verbs carry no inherent tone in isolation. Also p.61: 'The description of the sound system is yet to be completed' (= Omamor 1990).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the book. sec. 4.6.8 Tone p.70: 'Hoffmann (1973) marks two tones and a downstep in his examples. Until a better analysis emerges, we shall assume that Professor Hoffmann is correct.' sec. 3.5 p.48: SWE languages generally have no downdrift but downstep in some cases and a final-low-raising phenomenon. Informant Solomon Enunuaye (p.15); author notes his Okpe data were lost in 1980 and only recently replaced (p.69).
Bibliographic only; classification Edoid > South-Western; 5 descriptive refs, all phonology/specific-feature articles, no grammar.
